notes.front: What is the National Response Center (NRC), in hazmat incident reporting?
notes.back: The centre that receives the telephone notice of certain hazmat incidents: 800-424-8802 (toll free) or 202-267-2675 (toll call).
notes.explanation: Two numbers are given: one toll free and one toll call.
notes.example: Like calling the emergency services, but this is the notice the regulations require, as soon as practical and within 12 hours.
notes.evidence: must provide notice by telephone to the National Response Center (NRC) on 800–424–8802 (toll free) or 202– 267–2675 (toll call).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 171.15(a), PDF p. 42

notes.front: Who must give telephone notice of a reportable hazmat incident, and by when?
notes.back: Each person in physical possession of the material, as soon as practical and no later than 12 hours after the incident.
notes.explanation: The deadline is 12 hours at most, and sooner if practical.
notes.evidence: As soon as practical but no later than 12 hours after the occurrence of any incident described in paragraph (b) of this section, each person in physical possession of the hazardous material must provide notice by telephone
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 171.15(a), PDF p. 42

notes.front: Which harm to people, caused directly by a hazardous material in transport, makes a telephone report to the NRC required?
notes.back: A person is killed, or a person receives an injury requiring admittance to a hospital.
notes.explanation: The rule counts loading, unloading and temporary storage as part of transportation.
notes.evidence: during the course of transportation in commerce (including loading, unloading, and temporary storage): (1) As a direct result of a hazardous material— (i) A person is killed; (ii) A person receives an injury requiring admittance to a hospital;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 171.15(b)(1)(i)–(ii), PDF p. 42

notes.front: How long must a public evacuation caused by a hazardous material last to make an NRC telephone report required?
notes.explanation: The evacuation must be of the general public and a direct result of the hazardous material.
notes.evidence: (iii) The general public is evacuated for one hour or more;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 171.15(b)(1)(iii), PDF p. 42

notes.front: When does closing a road or transport facility make an NRC telephone report required?
notes.back: When a major transportation artery or facility is closed or shut down for one hour or more, as a direct result of a hazardous material.
notes.explanation: It is one of the § 171.15(b)(1) consequences that trigger the call, alongside deaths, hospital admissions and evacuations.
notes.evidence: (iv) A major transportation artery or facility is closed or shut down for one hour or more;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 171.15(b)(1)(iv), PDF p. 43

notes.front: A drum falls from a truck and leaks; police close the interstate for 90 minutes. Nobody is hurt. What must the carrier do?
notes.back: D: telephone the NRC within 12 hours, and file the written incident report within 30 days.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, because nobody was hurt
B) Only a written report within 30 days
C) Telephone the NRC within 30 days
D) Telephone the NRC within 12 hours and file the written report within 30 days
notes.choicesExplained: A: a closure of one hour or more is enough on its own. B: the closure also triggers the telephone notice. C: the telephone notice is due within 12 hours, not 30 days.
notes.explanation: A major artery closed for an hour or more triggers the call, and each person making a telephone report must also make the written report.
notes.evidence: Each person making a report under this section must also make the report required by § 171.16 of this subpart.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 171.15(b)–(c), PDF p. 43

notes.front: Within what time must the written Hazardous Materials Incident Report (Form F 5800.1) be submitted?
notes.back: Within 30 days of discovery of the incident.
notes.explanation: The 30 days run from discovery of the incident, not from when it happened.
notes.evidence: must submit a Hazardous Materials Incident Report on DOT Form F 5800.1 (01/2004) within 30 days of discovery of the incident:
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 171.16(a), PDF p. 43

notes.front: Besides incidents needing a telephone report, what are two incidents that need a written incident report?
notes.back: Any two of: an unintentional hazmat release; a hazardous waste discharge; structural damage to a specification cargo tank of 1,000 gallons or more.
notes.explanation: A written report can be due even when no telephone notice was required.
notes.evidence: (2) An unintentional release of a hazardous material or the discharge of any quantity of hazardous waste; (3) A specification cargo tank with a capacity of 1,000 gallons or greater containing any hazardous material suffers structural damage to the lading retention system
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 171.16(a)(2)–(4), PDF p. 43

notes.front: At a depot, a worker finds that a drum of a Packing Group II Class 3 liquid has leaked about 5 litres onto the trailer floor. No one is hurt and nothing is closed. What report is due?
notes.back: B: a written incident report within 30 days; the incident does not meet the telephone-report criteria.
notes.choices:
A) A telephone call to the NRC within 12 hours only
B) A written incident report within 30 days
C) No report, because the release was small
D) Both a telephone call and a written report
notes.choicesExplained: A: none of the § 171.15(b) telephone triggers occurred, and the written report is still due. C: the small-release exception in § 171.16(d)(2) covers limited quantities and Packing Group III material, not this Packing Group II liquid. D: the telephone notice is required only for the § 171.15(b) incidents.
notes.explanation: An unintentional release needs the written report unless a § 171.16(d) exception fits, and a Packing Group II material does not; the telephone notice depends on consequences such as death, hospital admission, evacuation or closure.
notes.evidence: (2) An unintentional release of a hazardous material or the discharge of any quantity of hazardous waste;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 171.16(a)(2), PDF p. 43

notes.front: What is the maximum civil penalty for each knowing violation of the hazmat regulations, and the higher cap?
notes.back: $102,348 per violation; $238,809 if the violation results in death, serious illness, severe injury or substantial destruction of property.
notes.explanation: Both caps apply per violation; which one applies depends on the harm the violation causes.
notes.evidence: is liable for a civil penalty of not more than $102,348 for each violation, except the maximum civil penalty is $238,809 if the violation results in death, serious illness, or severe injury to any person or substantial destruction of property.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 107 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 107.329(a), PDF p. 25

notes.front: An inspector finds that a hazmat employer let an untrained employee prepare shipments. What is the lowest civil penalty that may be assessed for that violation?
notes.back: $617, the minimum civil penalty for violations relating to training.
notes.explanation: For every other kind of violation there is no minimum.
notes.evidence: There is no minimum civil penalty, except for a minimum civil penalty of $617 for violations relating to training.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 107 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 107.329(a), PDF p. 25

notes.front: How is a continuing violation counted for civil penalties?
notes.back: Each day of a continuing violation is subject to its own civil penalty, except for violations relating to packaging manufacture or qualification.
notes.explanation: So a violation left uncorrected for days can be penalised day by day.
notes.evidence: each violation of the HMR and each day of a continuing violation (except for violations relating to packaging manufacture or qualification) is subject to a civil penalty of up to $102,348 or $238,809
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 107 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), Part 107, subpart D, appendix A (Guidelines for Civil Penalties), PDF p. 41
